questions.question: When data is replicated across several machines, what is the core difficulty once the data starts changing?

options.text: Each change must reach every replica, and until it does the copies disagree
Every read must contact all replicas, so reads become slower than on one machine
Even unchanging data drifts apart across replicas and must be re-copied continually
Each extra copy multiplies storage cost, which is the main algorithmic obstacle

questions.explanation: If replicated data never changed, replication would be a one-time copy. All the difficulty lies in handling changes: every write must be propagated to every replica, and until it arrives, different replicas can return different values. Single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication are different answers to how to propagate those changes. A read needs only one copy, static data does not drift, and storage cost is a resource cost rather than the algorithmic problem.

questions.question: In distributed data systems, what is replication?

options.text: Keeping a copy of the same data on several networked machines
Splitting data across multiple machines so each holds a subset
Keeping multiple versions of the same data on one machine
Copying data between a database and a data warehouse

questions.explanation: Replication keeps the same logical data on multiple machines. It supports availability, lower read latency, disconnected operation, and read scaling; partitioning instead splits different subsets of data across machines.

questions.question: Why would you want to replicate data? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: To keep data geographically close to your users, and thus reduce latency
To allow the system to continue working even if some of its parts have failed, and thus increase availability
To scale out the number of machines that can serve read queries, and thus increase read throughput
To store more data than fits on a single machine, and thus increase total storage capacity

questions.explanation: Replication copies the same logical dataset onto multiple machines. Splitting a dataset so that it can exceed one machine's capacity is partitioning, a different scaling technique.

optionExplanations.a: Placing a replica near its readers shortens the network round trip, so geographically distributed copies can directly reduce user-visible read latency.
optionExplanations.b: Redundant copies let another replica continue serving after a machine or site fails, provided the system can route around the failed component.
optionExplanations.c: Followers can serve read-only traffic in parallel, increasing aggregate read throughput even though writes may still pass through one leader.
optionExplanations.d: Copying the whole dataset does not increase the size one replica can hold; dividing different records across machines is partitioning rather than replication.

questions.question: When replication is reasoned about on its own, before partitioning is introduced, what is assumed about dataset size?

options.text: That the dataset is small enough for every machine to hold it all
That the dataset exceeds one machine, so each replica holds only a subset
That the dataset fits in memory on every node, so durability needs no disk
That no assumption about dataset size is needed, because replication is independent of volume

questions.explanation: To study replication in isolation, assume each machine can hold a full copy of the dataset. Partitioning (sharding) a dataset that is too big for one machine is a separate technique layered on later; real systems often combine both, replicating each partition. Fitting on a machine is not the same as fitting in memory, and replicas still need durable storage either way.

questions.question: When is replicating data across machines easy, and why?

options.text: When the data never changes, because it only has to be copied to every node once
When every replica runs the same software version, because the log format then matches
When replication is synchronous, because waiting for followers removes all coordination
When the dataset is small enough to fit in memory, because copying it is then quick

questions.explanation: If the data is static, you copy it to every node once and are done. The hard part of replication is propagating ongoing changes: ordering them, coping with lag and failed nodes, and resolving conflicts. Synchronous replication does not remove these problems; it trades lag for writes that block when a follower is unavailable. A small or in-memory dataset still changes, and matching software versions only helps with log compatibility.

questions.question: Which three algorithms for replicating changes between nodes do almost all distributed databases use?

options.text: Single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication
Synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous replication
Statement-based, write-ahead-log shipping and logical-log replication
Hash-based, range-based and round-robin replication

questions.explanation: Single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication differ in which nodes accept writes: one leader, several leaders, or any replica. Synchronous versus asynchronous is a timing choice that applies within these algorithms. Statement-based, WAL and logical-log replication are ways of encoding the replication log in leader-based systems. Hash, range and round-robin describe how data is partitioned, not how changes are replicated.

questions.question: In a replicated database, whether a write waits for follower confirmation (synchronous versus asynchronous replication) is one basic trade-off, often exposed as a configuration option. Which other trade-off is commonly configured alongside it?

options.text: How to handle replicas that have failed
Which order followers apply the leader's writes in
Whether the leader keeps a full copy of the data
Whether replicas must eventually hold the same data

questions.explanation: Choosing synchronous or asynchronous replication, and deciding how to handle failed replicas, are both durability, latency and availability trade-offs; databases expose them as settings whose details vary but whose principles are similar. The others are not options: followers must apply writes in the leader's order or they diverge, the leader holds a full copy by definition, and every replication scheme must make replicas eventually converge.

questions.question: Why have the fundamental principles of replication changed little since the 1970s?

options.text: Because the fundamental constraints of networks have stayed the same
Because the original algorithms were proven optimal for every workload
Because storage and network hardware have not improved since then
Because replication research stopped once relational databases dominated

questions.explanation: Replication must cope with the same basic facts as in the 1970s: messages can be delayed or lost, nodes fail, and no node has an instant global view. Hardware has become vastly faster, but those network constraints remain, so the principles studied then still apply. What changed is mainstream use of distributed databases; many developers long assumed a single-node database, which led to misunderstandings such as those around eventual consistency. Research did not stop: chain replication, for example, is more recent.

questions.question: What is a replica in a distributed database?

options.text: Any node that stores a copy of the database, leader included
A node that holds a disjoint subset of the data, chosen by key
A periodic offline backup copy taken on a fixed schedule
Specifically a read-only follower, as opposed to the leader

questions.explanation: Every node that stores a copy of the database is a replica, and that includes the leader in leader-based replication. Every write must be processed by every replica, otherwise the replicas no longer contain the same data. A node holding only a subset of keys is a partition, and a periodic backup is not continuously updated by the replication stream.

questions.question: Which statements describe how leader-based (single-leader) replication works? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One of the replicas is designated the leader; when clients want to write to the database they must send their requests to the leader, which first writes the new data to its local storage

The other replicas are followers; whenever the leader writes new data to its local storage it also sends the data change to all of its followers as part of a replication log or change stream, and each follower applies all writes in the same order as they were processed on the leader
Reads can go to the leader or any follower, but writes are only accepted on the leader — the followers are read-only from the client's point of view
Followers may accept writes directly from clients provided they forward each one to the leader, which then re-broadcasts it to the remaining followers in its own log order

questions.explanation: Leader-based replication makes one replica the single entry point for writes. The leader writes each change to its local storage and sends it to every follower through a replication log or change stream; followers apply the changes in the same order the leader processed them, which keeps their copies consistent with the leader. Any replica may serve reads, but clients cannot write to followers. Routing client writes through followers is not part of the basic scheme.

optionExplanations.a: The leader is the serialization point for writes: clients send changes there first, and its local write establishes the order followers must reproduce.
optionExplanations.b: Followers consume the leader's change stream and apply entries in leader order, which makes deterministic changes converge to the leader's state.
optionExplanations.c: Leader-based replication deliberately separates read and write routing: replicas may serve reads, but client writes are accepted only by the leader.
optionExplanations.d: Allowing followers to accept independent client writes would create multiple write authorities or merely proxy the request; it is not a step of basic leader-based replication.

questions.question: Which alternative names exist for leader-based replication and its roles? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The scheme is also known as active/passive replication
The leader is also called the primary
Followers are also called read replicas, secondaries, or hot standbys
The scheme is also known as quorum replication

questions.explanation: Leader-based replication is also called active/passive replication; the leader is also called the primary; followers are also called read replicas, secondaries or hot standbys. Quorum replication belongs to leaderless (Dynamo-style) systems, where any replica accepts writes and operations wait for a configured number of responses. Standby terminology varies by product: in PostgreSQL a hot standby serves client reads, while a warm standby replays changes without serving queries.

optionExplanations.a: Active/passive describes the same write asymmetry: one active replica accepts changes while passive replicas follow its log and stand ready to take over.
optionExplanations.b: Primary is a widely used synonym for the replica that accepts and orders writes; leader is the more general term for the same role.
optionExplanations.c: Read replica, secondary and hot standby all describe follower roles, though products differ on whether a standby may serve client queries.
optionExplanations.d: Quorum replication is a different coordination model in which operations wait for subsets of replicas; it is not another name for leader-based replication.

questions.question: Which relational databases have leader-based replication built in? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: PostgreSQL, from version 9.0 onward
MySQL
Oracle Data Guard and SQL Server's AlwaysOn Availability Groups
SQLite, plus Microsoft Access and dBase

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL (since version 9.0), MySQL, Oracle Data Guard and SQL Server's AlwaysOn Availability Groups all ship leader-based replication as a built-in feature: one node accepts writes and streams its changes to followers. It is also used beyond relational databases, in MongoDB, RethinkDB and Espresso, in message brokers such as Kafka and RabbitMQ highly available queues, and in replicated block devices such as DRBD. SQLite, Access and dBase are embedded or desktop databases without built-in leader–follower replication.

optionExplanations.a: PostgreSQL has shipped built-in streaming leader–follower replication since version 9.0, making the version qualification part of the accurate product claim.
optionExplanations.b: MySQL's traditional replication architecture designates a write source and replays its change log on replicas, which is leader-based replication.
optionExplanations.c: Oracle Data Guard and SQL Server AlwaysOn Availability Groups both maintain replicas around a primary write authority and support failover.
optionExplanations.d: SQLite, Access and dBase are embedded or desktop databases that run inside one application and ship no built-in leader-follower replication; replicating them requires external tools.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, is the choice between synchronous and asynchronous replication configurable?

options.text: Often configurable in relational databases; hardcoded in many others
Usually hardcoded in relational databases; configurable in most others
It is never configurable, being a fixed property of the replication algorithm
It is configurable only in leaderless systems, never in leader-based ones

questions.explanation: In relational databases, whether followers are synchronous or asynchronous is often a configuration option, while many other systems hardcode one mode into their architecture. So it is neither universally configurable nor universally fixed, relational databases are where the setting is most commonly exposed rather than the exception, and it is not specific to leaderless systems.

questions.question: In leader-based replication with a synchronous follower, the leader waits for that follower to confirm it received a write. Which actions does the leader hold back until the confirmation arrives?

options.text: Reporting success to the client and making the write visible to other clients
Reporting success to the client and writing the change to its own local storage
Making the write visible to other clients and compacting its replication log
Reporting success to the client only; other clients may see the write at once

questions.explanation: With a synchronous follower, the leader waits for the follower's confirmation before reporting success to the user and before making the write visible to other clients. That way no client is told about, or can observe, a write that exists only on the leader; if the leader then crashes, the write is still on the follower. The leader writes to its own storage first, so waiting is about the follower, and log compaction is unrelated.

questions.question: In asynchronous leader-based replication, which statements about follower lag are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Most databases apply changes to followers in under a second, but there is no guarantee of how long it takes
A follower recovering from a failure can fall several minutes or more behind the leader
Operating near maximum capacity, or network problems between nodes, can leave a follower minutes behind
An idle leader causes lag, because followers only poll for changes periodically

questions.explanation: Asynchronous followers are usually less than a second behind, but no protocol bound guarantees that delay. Recovery, overload or network trouble can therefore stretch lag to minutes or longer.

optionExplanations.a: Sub-second lag is a common observation, not a guarantee; asynchronous replication has no fixed upper bound on how long a follower may remain behind.
optionExplanations.b: A recovering follower may need to replay a large backlog or restore a snapshot before it approaches the leader's current log position.
optionExplanations.c: Overload slows log generation and application, while network trouble delays delivery, so either condition can stretch replication lag to minutes.
optionExplanations.d: An idle leader creates fewer changes to replicate rather than a backlog; follower lag is not normally caused by periodic polling during leader idleness.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, what are the main advantage and disadvantage of making a follower synchronous?

options.text: The follower is guaranteed up to date; if it stops responding, writes cannot proceed
Write throughput is higher; a failover can lose writes already acknowledged
Write latency is lower; the follower may permanently diverge from the leader
Write conflicts become impossible; a majority of followers must stay online

questions.explanation: A synchronous follower confirms each write before the leader acknowledges it, so it is guaranteed to hold an up-to-date copy consistent with the leader, and the data survives a sudden leader failure. The cost is availability: if that follower crashes, is cut off by a network fault or simply does not respond, the leader must block all writes until it is available again. Synchronous waiting increases latency rather than lowering it, and it requires one specific follower, not a majority.

questions.question: Why is it impractical for all followers to be synchronous, and what is used in practice?

options.text: One node outage would block all writes; so one follower is synchronous, the rest asynchronous
The leader cannot track more than one follower; so all followers are made asynchronous
Network bandwidth is insufficient; so a quorum of followers acknowledges each write
Followers would conflict with one another; so the replicas are arranged in a chain

questions.explanation: If every follower were synchronous, the leader would wait for all of them, so any single node failing or slowing down would halt all writes. In practice, enabling synchronous replication usually means one follower is synchronous and the others are asynchronous; if the synchronous one becomes unavailable or slow, an asynchronous follower is made synchronous. This semi-synchronous setup guarantees an up-to-date copy on at least two nodes, the leader and the synchronous follower.

questions.question: What is lost and what is gained when leader-based replication is fully asynchronous?

options.text: Confirmed writes can be lost if the leader fails; writes continue even when all followers lag
Writes are always durable but reads may be stale; the leader gains lower read latency
Every acknowledged write survives a failure; the leader simply gains write throughput
Writes are lost only if a follower fails; the cluster gains a simpler failover process

questions.explanation: In a fully asynchronous configuration the leader acknowledges a write before any follower has it. If the leader fails and is not recoverable, writes not yet replicated are lost, so a write is not guaranteed durable even if it has been confirmed to the client. The benefit is that the leader can keep processing writes even if all of its followers have fallen behind or are unavailable. Follower failures, by contrast, do not lose data, because the leader still has it.

questions.question: Although it weakens durability, asynchronous leader-based replication is widely used. Under which conditions especially? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Especially if there are many followers
Especially if the followers are geographically distributed
Especially if the workload is read-only
Especially if durability is the top priority

questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication weakens durability, yet it is widely used when there are many followers or when they are geographically distributed. With many followers, waiting for all of them makes each write depend on more machines; with distant followers, each write would pay wide-area round trips. Asynchronous propagation keeps the leader responsive in both cases.

optionExplanations.a: Waiting synchronously for many followers makes each write depend on more machines, increasing latency and the probability that one slow follower blocks progress.
optionExplanations.b: Geographically distant followers add wide-area round trips to the write path, so asynchronous propagation avoids making every write pay inter-datacenter latency.
optionExplanations.c: A read-only workload produces no new writes to acknowledge, so it does not explain why asynchronous write replication would be chosen.
optionExplanations.d: When preservation of every acknowledged write is the overriding priority, asynchronous replication is a poor fit because recent acknowledged writes can be lost on failover.

questions.question: Which variant of synchronous replication was researched to avoid losing data on leader failure while keeping good performance and availability, and has been implemented in Microsoft Azure Storage?

options.text: Chain replication
Statement-based replication
Hinted-handoff replication
Trigger-based replication

questions.explanation: Chain replication is a variant of synchronous replication: replicas are arranged in a sequence, writes travel along the chain, and a write is acknowledged once it has passed through every replica, so acknowledged writes are not lost when one node fails. It has been implemented in a few systems such as Microsoft Azure Storage. Statement-based and trigger-based replication are ways of encoding or capturing changes, and hinted handoff is a leaderless mechanism for temporarily storing writes on substitute nodes.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, why is simply copying the leader's data files to a new node not sufficient to set up a new follower?

options.text: Because clients keep writing, so the file copy would be internally inconsistent
Because the on-disk file formats differ between nodes running different versions
Because copying a large data directory would take far too long to be practical
Because the copied files would carry the wrong ownership and permissions

questions.explanation: Clients keep writing while the copy runs, so a plain file copy captures different parts of the database at different moments, and the result may not be a coherent state. Locking the database during the copy would make the files consistent but would stop writes, which goes against high availability. Instead, a consistent snapshot tied to a replication-log position is copied and the later changes are replayed. Version differences and copy duration are operational concerns, not the reason a copy is incorrect.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, which steps set up a new follower without downtime? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Take a consistent snapshot of the leader and record its exact replication-log position
Copy the snapshot to the new follower
Replay every change after the snapshot position until caught up, then continue processing new changes
Stop all leader writes until the follower is byte-identical, then reopen the application

questions.explanation: The snapshot establishes a consistent starting state and exact log position. The follower copies it, replays the later log entries, and then follows new writes continuously. The leader keeps accepting writes throughout, so application downtime is unnecessary.

optionExplanations.a: A consistent snapshot plus its exact log position gives the new follower a coherent base and an unambiguous point from which to resume replication.
optionExplanations.b: Copying that snapshot transfers the bulk of the existing database without forcing the follower to reconstruct the entire history one write at a time.
optionExplanations.c: Replaying changes after the recorded position closes the gap created during snapshot copying, after which the follower can consume the live stream.
optionExplanations.d: Stopping all writes is unnecessary when snapshot position and log replay are available; that misconception confuses a simple file copy with an online bootstrap protocol.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, why must the system tolerate individual nodes going down even if its hardware were perfectly reliable?

options.text: Nodes are also taken down on purpose, e.g. rebooted to install a kernel security patch
Followers shut themselves down automatically whenever they fall behind the leader
Replication protocols require every node to restart periodically to resync its log
Leaders step down after a fixed number of writes so that leadership rotates

questions.explanation: Nodes go down unexpectedly due to faults, but just as likely due to planned maintenance such as rebooting a machine to install a kernel security patch. Being able to reboot individual nodes without downtime is a big operational advantage, so the goal is to keep the whole system running despite individual node outages and to keep their impact small. Followers do not shut themselves down when lagging, and leaders do not rotate on a write count.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, how does a follower recover after it crashes or its network link to the leader is briefly interrupted, and why is this relatively easy?

options.text: Its local log shows the last transaction it applied; it asks the leader for later changes
It must be rebuilt from a fresh snapshot of the leader's database every time it restarts
The leader must replay its entire replication log to it, starting from the very first entry
An election chooses a new leader, and the failed follower is discarded from the cluster

questions.explanation: Each follower keeps a log of the data changes it received from the leader on its local disk. After a crash or interruption it knows from that log the last transaction processed, connects to the leader, requests all changes since then, applies them, and has caught up; this is catch-up recovery. It is easy because the follower has a known resume point and the leader is still there to supply the missing changes. Leader failure is harder because a new leader must be chosen and the system reconfigured.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, which actions does failover after a leader failure require? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: One of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader
Clients need to be reconfigured to send their writes to the new leader
The other followers need to start consuming data changes from the new leader
All of the data must be re-replicated from scratch onto every remaining replica

questions.explanation: Failover requires three coordinated changes: promote a follower, redirect client writes, and make the other followers consume from the new leader. Systems may perform those steps manually or automatically.

optionExplanations.a: A surviving follower must become the new write authority so the system has one place to accept and order subsequent writes.
optionExplanations.b: Promotion alone is insufficient because clients may keep sending writes to the failed or recovered old leader; routing must identify the replacement.
optionExplanations.c: The remaining followers must switch their replication source or they will continue waiting for a leader that no longer supplies changes.
optionExplanations.d: Existing replicas already contain most of the dataset and can reconcile missing entries; rebuilding every copy from scratch would make failover needlessly slow.

questions.question: In automatic failover for leader-based replication, how do most systems decide that the leader has failed?

options.text: A timeout: a leader silent for some period, say 30 seconds, is assumed dead
The leader sends a final shutdown message before failing, which followers wait to receive
A diagnostic probe determines whether the leader crashed, lost power or was partitioned
Followers compare replication-log positions and declare the leader dead if they differ

questions.explanation: Crashes, power outages and network problems all look the same from outside, and there is no foolproof way to tell what went wrong. So most systems simply use a timeout: nodes exchange messages frequently, and a node that does not respond for some period (such as 30 seconds) is assumed dead. A crashed node cannot send a farewell message, a remote probe cannot reliably diagnose the cause, and log positions differ routinely because of normal replication lag.

questions.question: During failover in leader-based replication, how can the new leader be chosen?

options.text: By majority election among the remaining replicas, or by a controller node
The longest-running replica always takes over automatically, with no agreement needed
Each follower independently promotes itself once it stops hearing from the leader
The client that issues the next write decides which replica becomes the leader

questions.explanation: A new leader can be elected by a majority of the remaining replicas or appointed by a previously elected controller node. The best candidate is usually the replica with the most up-to-date changes from the old leader, which minimizes lost writes. Getting all nodes to agree on one new leader is a consensus problem; replicas promoting themselves independently, or clients choosing, risks two leaders.

questions.question: After failover in leader-based replication, what is the specific danger if the old leader comes back online?

options.text: It may still believe it is the leader and must be made to step down
It will have lost all of its data and must be rebuilt from a leader snapshot
It will automatically overwrite the new leader's log with its own longer one
It will refuse to rejoin the cluster until an administrator intervenes

questions.explanation: When the old leader recovers, it may still believe that it is the leader, not realizing that the other replicas have forced it to step down. If it kept accepting writes there would be two leaders (split brain), so the system must ensure that it becomes a follower and recognizes the new leader. A recovering node normally still has its data, it does not automatically overwrite the new leader, and it is not inherently barred from rejoining; the danger is stale belief in its own leadership.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, what data-loss risk does asynchronous replication create during failover?

options.text: The new leader may lack writes the old leader acknowledged, and those are usually discarded
The old leader's unreplicated writes are always merged back in when it rejoins the cluster
The new leader first replays the old leader's full log from disk, so nothing is lost
All writes are refused until the old leader returns, so no data can be lost

questions.explanation: With asynchronous replication the leader may acknowledge writes before any follower has them. If it fails, the promoted follower lacks those writes, and the new leader may accept conflicting writes in the meantime. When the old leader rejoins, the most common solution is to discard its unreplicated writes, which may violate clients' durability expectations. The failed leader's log is not available to replay, and refusing writes until it returns would defeat the purpose of failover.

questions.question: A MySQL leader fails over to an out-of-date follower, and a Redis store keyed by MySQL's autoincrementing primary keys is used alongside it. What goes wrong?

options.text: The new leader reissues primary keys, so Redis keys now point at the wrong rows
A split brain lets two leaders accept conflicting writes, corrupting Redis keys
Redis evicts its entries, so every write from the preceding hour is lost outright
The failover timeout is too short, causing repeated and unnecessary failovers

questions.explanation: The promoted follower was out of date, so its autoincrementing counter lagged behind the old leader's and it reassigned primary keys the old leader had already used. Redis still held entries under those keys for the old rows, so the two stores became inconsistent and some private data was shown to the wrong users. Discarding the old leader's writes is especially dangerous when other storage systems outside the database are coordinated with its contents.

questions.question: What does split brain mean in leader-based replication?

options.text: Two nodes simultaneously believe that they are the leader
A node loses its data and must be rebuilt from a snapshot
Followers diverge because they apply writes in different orders
A network partition leaves no node able to accept any writes

questions.explanation: Split brain is when two nodes both believe they are the leader, for example after a failover in which the old leader does not realize it has been replaced. If both accept writes and there is no process for resolving conflicts, data is likely to be lost or corrupted. As a safety catch, some systems shut down one node when two leaders are detected (fencing, or STONITH); if that mechanism is badly designed, both nodes can end up shut down.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, what is the trade-off when choosing the timeout after which a leader is declared dead?

options.text: A long timeout delays recovery; a short one causes unnecessary failovers
A long timeout causes unnecessary failovers; a short one delays recovery
The timeout only affects false alarms, not how long recovery takes
Shorter is always better, because a failover reduces load on the system

questions.explanation: A longer timeout means a longer time to recovery when the leader really has failed. A timeout that is too short causes unnecessary failovers, for example when a temporary load spike or a network glitch delays responses. If the system is already struggling with high load or network problems, an unnecessary failover is likely to make things worse, not better. Because there are no easy answers, some operations teams prefer to perform failovers manually.

questions.question: Failover in leader-based replication exposes which fundamental problems of distributed systems?

options.text: Node failures, unreliable networks, and consistency/durability/availability trade-offs
Write amplification, compaction and read amplification in the storage engine
Choosing a multi-leader topology, conflict resolvers and quorum sizes
Schema evolution, data encoding formats and serialization libraries

questions.explanation: Failover must infer that a node failed from incomplete network evidence, choose exactly one replacement, and decide what happens to unreplicated writes. Those are the fundamental distributed-systems problems of node failures, unreliable networks, and trade-offs around replica consistency, durability, availability and latency. Storage-engine amplification and data encoding are single-node concerns, and topologies, conflict resolvers and quorum sizes are design parameters of multi-leader and leaderless systems.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, what is statement-based replication?

options.text: The leader logs each write statement, and followers re-execute those statements
The leader sends its write-ahead log to followers, which apply it byte for byte
The leader sends row-level records of changed column values to followers
Followers periodically poll the leader and copy any rows that have changed

questions.explanation: In statement-based replication the leader logs every write request it executes, such as each INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, and sends that statement log to followers, which parse and execute each SQL statement as if a client had sent it. Because the statement is re-executed rather than its effect copied, every replica must compute the same result, so nondeterminism breaks it. Shipping the write-ahead log and shipping row-level records are the alternative methods.

questions.question: Which ways can statement-based replication break down? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Nondeterministic functions — any statement calling NOW() to get the current date and time or RAND() to get a random number is likely to generate a different value on each replica

Order dependence — if statements use an autoincrementing column or depend on the existing data (such as UPDATE ... WHERE some condition), they must be executed in exactly the same order on each replica, which can be limiting when there are multiple concurrently executing transactions

Side effects — statements that have side effects such as triggers, stored procedures and user-defined functions may result in different side effects occurring on each replica, unless the side effects are absolutely deterministic
Encoding differences — a statement written against one character set cannot be parsed by a replica configured with another, so the follower skips the write and logs a warning to its error log instead

questions.explanation: A replicated statement is safe only if every replica produces the same effect. Time/random functions, order-dependent updates and nondeterministic side effects can each make replicas diverge.

optionExplanations.a: NOW() and RAND() are evaluated independently on each replica, so replaying identical SQL text can produce different stored values.
optionExplanations.b: Autoincrement values and data-dependent predicates depend on preceding state, so a different concurrent execution order can make the statement affect different rows.
optionExplanations.c: Triggers and user-defined code may consult local state or external effects, so statement replay is safe only when every side effect is deterministic.
optionExplanations.d: Character-set compatibility can be an operational concern, but the claimed automatic skip-and-warning behavior is not a fundamental failure mode of statement-based replication.

questions.question: How can statement-based replication handle a nondeterministic function call?

options.text: The leader substitutes the call's fixed return value into the logged statement
Followers re-run the call, which gives the same result because SQL functions are pure
Each follower skips any statement that contains a nondeterministic function
Followers evaluate the function using a clock synchronized with the leader

questions.explanation: The leader can replace a nondeterministic call such as NOW() or RAND() with the fixed value it obtained when it logs the statement, so every follower executes the statement with the same value. Re-running the call on each follower does not work, because NOW() and RAND() are not pure: each replica would read its own clock or random generator and store a different value. Skipping the statement would make replicas diverge, and even synchronized clocks do not make RAND() agree. Because there are many such edge cases, other methods are generally preferred: MySQL switches to row-based replication when a statement is nondeterministic, and VoltDB keeps statement-based replication safe by requiring transactions to be deterministic.

questions.question: Log-structured (LSM-tree) and B-tree storage engines can both support write-ahead log (WAL) shipping for replication. What property of these engines makes that possible?

options.text: Both engines keep an append-only byte log of every write
Both engines store table rows on disk in exactly the same physical format
Both engines already expose a logical, row-level change stream to clients
Both engines organize their storage into pages of one fixed size

questions.explanation: In a log-structured engine the log is the main storage; in a B-tree every modification is first written to a write-ahead log so the index can be restored after a crash. Either way there is an append-only sequence of bytes containing every write, so the leader can send that same log to followers, which build exact copies of its data structures. Because the log records which bytes changed in which disk blocks, this also couples replication to the storage engine's format.

questions.question: Which databases use WAL shipping, and what is its main disadvantage?

options.text: PostgreSQL and Oracle; the log is tied to the storage engine's internals
MySQL and MongoDB; the log is too large to send over the network
Cassandra and Riak; the log cannot capture nondeterministic functions
PostgreSQL and MySQL; the log omits changes made by triggers

questions.explanation: A WAL records low-level storage changes, so replay is faithful and efficient. That same detail couples leader and follower to the storage engine's on-disk format, complicating version upgrades.

questions.question: In WAL-shipping replication, the log format is tied to the database's storage engine and software version. What operational impact does this have?

options.text: It makes rolling, zero-downtime upgrades of the database software difficult
It makes upgrades faster, because followers can skip parsing logical records
It forces every follower to be rebuilt from a fresh snapshot on each upgrade
None, because a failover always restarts every node on the same software build

questions.explanation: WAL records describe low-level storage changes whose format can vary by software version. A follower on another version may not understand them, so the usual rolling-upgrade pattern—followers first, failover, then the old leader—is often unavailable.

questions.question: In logical (row-based) log replication for a relational database, which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The replication log uses a format separate from the storage engine's physical representation and records writes at row granularity
For an inserted row, the log contains the new values of all columns
For a deleted row, the log identifies the row, typically by primary key, or by all old column values if there is no key
For an updated row, the log holds only the primary key, and followers fetch the new values from the leader

questions.explanation: A logical (row-based) log uses its own format, separate from the storage engine's physical representation, and describes writes at the granularity of a row. For an inserted row it contains the new values of all columns; for a deleted row, enough to identify the row (the primary key, or all old column values if the table has none); for an updated row, enough to identify the row plus the new values of all columns, or at least of those that changed. So a follower can apply an update from the log alone; it never needs to fetch values back from the leader. A transaction that modifies several rows produces several such records followed by a commit record; MySQL's binlog in row-based mode works this way.

optionExplanations.a: A logical log describes row-level database changes rather than storage-page mutations, which decouples replication from one engine's physical layout.
optionExplanations.b: An insert has no prior row on the follower, so the log must carry the new column values needed to construct that row.
optionExplanations.c: A delete must identify exactly which row to remove; a primary key is sufficient, while all old values may be needed when no key exists.
optionExplanations.d: Followers must be able to replay the log independently; fetching updated columns back from the leader would add coupling and fail when the leader is unavailable.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, which benefits come from using a logical replication log that is decoupled from the storage engine? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can more easily be kept backward compatible, allowing the leader and followers to run different versions of the database software, or even different storage engines

A logical log format is easier for external applications to parse — useful for sending database contents to an external system such as a data warehouse for offline analysis, or for building custom indexes and caches
It enables change data capture: an outside process can follow the stream of changes as they happen
It shrinks the replication log by roughly a factor of ten, because column names are replaced by numeric field tags

questions.explanation: A logical log describes row changes rather than bytes in disk blocks. That makes it easier to keep backward compatible, so the leader and followers can run different software versions or even different storage engines, which enables rolling upgrades. It is also easier for external applications to parse, which enables change data capture into data warehouses, caches and custom indexes. Smaller size is not one of its properties; row records can be larger than physical deltas.

optionExplanations.a: A stable logical format is less tied to storage internals, allowing replicas on different software versions or engines to interpret the same changes during upgrades.
optionExplanations.b: Row-oriented change records are understandable outside the storage engine, so warehouses, caches and custom indexes can consume them without decoding physical pages.
optionExplanations.c: Change data capture is precisely the practice of an external consumer following the logical change stream as committed updates occur.
optionExplanations.d: Logical logging is chosen for decoupling and interpretability, not for a guaranteed tenfold size reduction; verbose row values may even make some records larger.

questions.question: In which circumstances might you need trigger-based replication? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If you want to only replicate a subset of the data
If you want to replicate from one kind of database to another
If you need conflict resolution logic
If you need lower latency than the database's built-in replication

questions.explanation: Built-in replication is implemented by the database without application code. When you need more flexibility, such as replicating only a subset of data, replicating between different kinds of database, or custom conflict resolution, replication moves up to the application layer, for example with triggers that record changes for an external process to apply. That extra layer adds overhead rather than lowering latency.

optionExplanations.a: A trigger can record only selected table changes, enabling filtered replication when the database's built-in mechanism always copies the full stream.
optionExplanations.b: Writing changes into an application-readable table lets an external process transform and load them into a different database type.
optionExplanations.c: Application-specific conflict rules can be invoked from trigger-driven change handling when the native replication layer lacks the required resolution logic.
optionExplanations.d: Triggers add application and database work and are usually more fragile than built-in replication; they are not a general route to lower replication latency.

questions.question: In trigger-based replication, how is a database write captured for replication?

options.text: A trigger records the change in a separate table that an external process reads
A trigger pushes the change straight to remote replicas, with no intermediate table
A trigger rewrites the write-ahead log so that followers replay the change
A trigger blocks the write until every replica has applied it synchronously

questions.explanation: A trigger registers custom application code that runs automatically when a write occurs. It can log the change into a separate table, from which an external process reads it, applies any application logic, and replicates it to another system; Databus for Oracle and Bucardo for Postgres work like this. This is useful when built-in replication cannot express the required filtering, transformation or cross-database copying.

questions.question: How does trigger-based replication compare with a database's built-in replication?

options.text: Greater overhead and more bugs than built-in replication, but flexible
It is the preferred replication method for most production deployments today
It carries no measurable overhead, but it is completely inflexible in use
It is faster than WAL shipping, at the cost of weaker durability guarantees

questions.explanation: Triggers execute in the write path, so they add latency and can fail in application-specific ways that built-in replication avoids. Their advantage is flexibility: they can filter or transform data and replicate between different technologies.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, what is a read-scaling architecture?

options.text: Many followers serve reads, while all writes still go through the single leader
Writes are spread across replicas, so write throughput grows with each node
All reads go to the leader, and followers act only as standby copies
Reads and writes both scale linearly as more followers are added

questions.explanation: For workloads that are mostly reads with a small share of writes, you can create many followers and distribute read requests across them. This removes load from the leader and lets nearby replicas serve reads, and read capacity grows by adding followers. Writes do not scale this way, because every write must still go through the single leader.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, why does a read-scaling architecture with many followers only realistically work with asynchronous replication?

options.text: Because if all were synchronous, one node failure would block writes
Because synchronous replication cannot serve read queries from its followers
Because asynchronous replication is always faster, whatever the node count
Because followers have no mechanism for acknowledging a write to the leader

questions.explanation: With synchronous replication the leader must wait for every follower before a write succeeds, so a single node failure or network outage would make the whole system unavailable for writing. The more followers you add, the likelier it is that one is down, so a fully synchronous configuration becomes very unreliable. Read scaling therefore relies on asynchronous followers, which in turn may serve stale data. Synchronous followers can serve reads; the problem is write availability.

questions.question: In an asynchronously replicated database, what does eventual consistency promise?

options.text: Replicas converge if writes stop, but with no time bound
All replicas are always consistent within one second
Replicas converge within a bounded delay even while writes continue
Reads always return the most recent write

questions.explanation: If you stop writing to the database and wait, followers will eventually catch up and become consistent with the leader; that temporary inconsistency is called eventual consistency. The word 'eventually' is deliberately vague: there is no limit to how far a replica can fall behind, and while writes continue, replicas may never be identical at the same moment. It promises nothing about reading the latest value or about a fixed delay.

questions.question: Is eventual consistency specific to NoSQL databases?

options.text: No; asynchronously replicated relational databases are eventually consistent too
Yes; Werner Vogels coined the term to describe NoSQL stores only
Yes; relational replicas are always synchronous, so they cannot lag
No; but only leaderless systems can exhibit it, whatever their category

questions.explanation: Eventual consistency is a property of asynchronous replication: replicas may lag and converge later. The term was coined by Douglas Terry et al., popularized by Werner Vogels, and became a battle cry of NoSQL projects, but followers in an asynchronously replicated relational database have the same characteristics. Single-leader asynchronous replication, not only leaderless replication, produces it.

questions.question: In asynchronous leader-based replication, how large is replication lag in practice, and what is its upper bound?

options.text: Often under a second, with no upper bound in general
Always under one second, bounded by the replication timeout
Bounded by the configured maximum lag setting
Bounded at 30 seconds by the failover timeout

questions.explanation: Replication lag is the delay between a write happening on the leader and being reflected on a follower. In normal operation it may be only a fraction of a second, but if the system is near capacity or there is a network problem it can grow to several seconds or minutes, and in general there is no limit to how far a replica can fall behind. Failover timeouts and configuration settings do not bound it.

questions.question: In asynchronously replicated systems, which three guarantees address common replication-lag anomalies?

options.text: Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix reads
Quorum reads, fencing tokens, and conflict-free replicated datatypes
Split-brain prevention, synchronous durability, and lag monitoring
Read committed, snapshot isolation, and serializable isolation

questions.explanation: Each guarantee prevents a different user-visible surprise caused by reading from lagging followers: read-your-writes stops a user's own update from appearing to vanish, monotonic reads stops data from moving backward between successive reads, and consistent prefix reads stops an answer from appearing before the question it responds to. The other lists name fault-tolerance mechanisms or transaction isolation levels, not the replication-lag guarantees.

questions.question: In leader-based replication with asynchronous followers, how can a user fail to see data they have just submitted?

options.text: The write reached the leader, but the read hit a follower that hasn't received it yet
The write was routed to a follower, which forwarded it to the leader only after the read
The leader buffers the write in memory and persists it only after the user's next read
The read went to the leader, whose cache still held the value from before the write

questions.explanation: New data must be sent to the leader, but views can be served from a follower. With asynchronous replication, if the user reads shortly after writing, the new data may not yet have reached that follower, so it looks to the user as if their submission was lost. Preventing this requires read-after-write (read-your-writes) consistency. Clients do not write to followers in leader-based replication, the leader writes new data to its local storage before replicating it, and a read served by the leader reflects the leader's own writes, so none of those explains the anomaly.

questions.question: In a replicated database, what does read-after-write (read-your-writes) consistency guarantee, and what does it not?

options.text: The user always sees their own updates, with no promise about others'
It guarantees all users see all writes immediately
It guarantees the user sees other users' writes but not necessarily their own
It guarantees strong consistency across all replicas

questions.explanation: Read-after-write consistency protects a user's own session: after submitting an update, that user will not read an older version. It does not make every user's reads globally current.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, a simple way to provide read-after-write consistency is to read some data from the leader and the rest from followers. Which rule does this use?

options.text: Read anything the user may have modified, such as their own profile, from the leader
Read everything from the leader, and use followers only as standby copies
Read from whichever follower currently reports the lowest replication lag
Read from two different followers and return whichever result is newer

questions.explanation: When reading something the user may have modified, read it from the leader; otherwise read from a follower. For example, a social-network profile is normally editable only by its owner, so read the user's own profile from the leader and other users' profiles from followers. This requires knowing what might have been modified without querying it, and it stops working when most content is user-editable. The lowest-lag or newer-of-two followers may still lack the write, and reading everything from the leader gives up read scaling.

questions.question: In leader-based replication where most content is user-editable, which pair of time-based rules can provide read-after-write consistency?

options.text: Use the leader for a minute after the user's last update; skip followers a minute behind
Declare the leader dead after one minute without a response, then fail over to a follower
Expire cached pages a minute after creation, and end user sessions after a minute idle
Truncate the leader's log after one minute, and rebuild followers that miss entries

questions.explanation: If most things are editable, reading everything the user might have modified from the leader would negate read scaling. Instead, track the time of the user's last update and, for one minute afterward, serve that user's reads from the leader; and monitor follower lag, preventing queries on any follower more than one minute behind the leader. The first is a per-user window, the second a per-follower eligibility threshold. Failover timeouts, cache expiry and log truncation do not ensure a user sees their own writes.

questions.question: In leader-based replication, how can a client's remembered timestamp of its most recent write be used to provide read-after-write consistency?

options.text: Read from a replica caught up to that timestamp, or wait, or try another
Attach the timestamp to the read so that followers discard any data newer than it
Use the timestamp only to order that user's writes on the leader, not for reads
Have the leader stamp every read with its own clock, making clock skew irrelevant

questions.explanation: The client remembers the timestamp of its most recent write, and the system ensures that any replica serving that user's reads reflects updates at least up to that timestamp. If a replica is not sufficiently up to date, the read can be handled by another replica or wait until it catches up. The timestamp can be logical, such as a log sequence number, which avoids clock problems, or the system clock, in which case clock synchronization becomes critical.

questions.question: In single-leader replication with replicas spread across multiple datacenters, what extra complexity arises for read-after-write consistency?

options.text: Leader-bound requests must be routed to the leader's own datacenter
Routing is unaffected, because each datacenter keeps its own independent leader
Timestamps become meaningless across datacenters
Reads must be served from all datacenters simultaneously

questions.explanation: If freshness requires reading from the leader, the router must know which datacenter hosts that leader and may send the request across regions. That can add latency and complicate failover.

questions.question: Which statements about cross-device read-after-write consistency are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If a user enters information on one device, such as a desktop browser, and then views it on another, such as a mobile app, they should see what they entered
Approaches that remember the timestamp of the user's last update become harder, because one device doesn't know what updates happened on another; this metadata must be centralized
Different devices may reach different datacenters, e.g. home broadband versus cellular, so reads that require the leader may first need all of a user's devices routed to the same datacenter
Devices cannot share one user identity across platforms, so cross-device read-after-write is impossible and is abandoned in favour of per-device consistency

questions.explanation: A guarantee that spans devices needs shared session metadata, because one device does not know what another just wrote. Their requests may also enter through different networks, so routing must still reach the required leader or datacenter.

optionExplanations.a: Cross-device read-after-write extends the guarantee across sessions: a change submitted on one device must be visible when the same user reads on another.
optionExplanations.b: A per-device timestamp cannot communicate the other device's last write, so the service needs centralized user-level metadata or another shared version marker.
optionExplanations.c: Different access networks may route a user's devices to different datacenters, so leader-dependent reads require consistent user routing across those entry points.
optionExplanations.d: A shared authenticated user identity and centralized metadata can connect device sessions; cross-device consistency is difficult but not inherently impossible.

questions.question: In asynchronous leader-based replication, user A refreshes a page twice. The first read goes to a follower with little lag and shows a comment just posted by user B; the second goes to a more lagged follower, and the comment is gone. What anomaly is this?

options.text: A monotonic-reads violation: the later read sees an older state than the first
A read-your-writes violation: user A cannot see a write that user A made
A consistent-prefix violation: two causally related writes appear in the wrong order
A lost update: the comment was overwritten by a concurrent write from another user

questions.explanation: When successive reads go to different replicas with different lag, a later read can observe the system at an earlier point in time than a previous read, so data the user already saw disappears. Monotonic reads is the guarantee that one user's sequence of reads never goes backward like this. It is not read-your-writes, because user A did not make the write, and not consistent prefix, because only one write is involved; the comment still exists on the leader.

questions.question: Under replication lag, why is it worse for a reader to see a newly posted comment and then have it vanish on refresh than not to see it at all yet?

options.text: Vanishing makes time appear to go backward; an unseen comment just seems not yet posted
Not seeing it at first is worse, because the reader may then never learn of the comment
Both are equally bad, since each returns stale data, so neither is worth designing around
Neither matters, because users already expect some lag in a distributed system

questions.explanation: A stale first read merely delays discovering the comment; the reader has no reason to think anything is wrong. Seeing it and then losing it on refresh makes the system appear to move backward in time, which is confusing. Monotonic reads guarantees exactly this cannot happen: a user may read old data, but never older data after having read newer data.

questions.question: Where does monotonic reads sit relative to strong and eventual consistency, and what exactly does it rule out?

options.text: Between eventual and strong; it rules out reading older data after newer data
Stronger than strong consistency; it rules out every stale read for every user
Equivalent to eventual consistency; it rules out nothing beyond eventual convergence
Equivalent to strong consistency; it ensures every read returns the latest write

questions.explanation: Monotonic reads is a lesser guarantee than strong consistency but a stronger one than eventual consistency. A read may still return an old value, so it does not promise the latest write; what it rules out is one user making several reads in sequence and seeing time go backward, that is, reading older data after having previously read newer data. Eventual consistency alone allows exactly that anomaly when successive reads hit replicas with different lag.

questions.question: How are monotonic reads commonly implemented?

options.text: Always route a user's reads to one replica, e.g. by hashing the user ID
Route each read to a randomly chosen replica to spread the load evenly
Route each read to whichever follower reports the lowest lag at that moment
Have each replica rebuild from a fresh snapshot before serving a read

questions.explanation: Making each user always read from the same replica means that user sees a single replica's history, which never goes backward; different users can read from different replicas. The replica can be chosen by a hash of the user ID rather than randomly. Random routing is what causes the anomaly, and the lowest-lag follower can change between reads. If the chosen replica fails, the user's queries must be rerouted, and the replacement may be further behind.

questions.question: Mr. Poons asks Mrs. Cake how far into the future she can see, and she replies that it is usually about ten seconds. The two lines are stored in different partitions of a sharded database, and an observer reads them through followers; Mr. Poons's partition replicates with more lag. What is the causal relationship, and what can the observer see?

options.text: The answer depends on the question, but the observer may see the answer first
The lines are causally independent, so any order the observer sees is equally valid
The question depends on the answer, so the observer always sees the question first
The answer depends on the question, but lag delays both lines equally, keeping their order

questions.explanation: Mrs. Cake's reply exists because she heard the question, so the answer causally depends on it. If the partitions replicate independently and the question's partition lags more, an observer can read the answer before the question, as if she answered before being asked. Consistent prefix reads prevents this: anyone reading a sequence of writes sees them in the order they happened.

questions.question: What does consistent-prefix reads guarantee?

options.text: If a sequence of writes happens in a certain order, anyone reading them sees that order
Every read returns the most recently written value for each key, on every replica
A single user's successive reads never go backward in time, even across replicas
Each user always sees the updates they submitted themselves, even on followers

questions.explanation: Consistent prefix reads says that if writes happen in a certain order, anyone reading them sees them appear in the same order, so a reply is never visible before the question it answers. It is a particular problem in partitioned (sharded) databases, where partitions operate independently with no global ordering of writes. Returning the latest value is strong consistency, never going backward is monotonic reads, and seeing one's own updates is read-your-writes.

questions.question: In a partitioned (sharded) database, what two approaches can provide consistent prefix reads?

options.text: Put causally related writes in the same partition, or track causal dependencies
Attach a wall-clock timestamp to each write, and sort every read result by it
Add more followers per partition, or reduce the number of replicas read per query
Route each user's reads to one replica, chosen by hashing the user ID

questions.explanation: If causally related writes go to the same partition, that partition's single ordered replication stream preserves their order. When that cannot be done efficiently, algorithms that explicitly track causal dependencies let a reader avoid exposing an answer before its question. Wall-clock timestamps are unreliable for ordering across nodes, more followers do not create ordering, and hashing users to one replica gives monotonic reads but not cross-partition ordering.

questions.question: When building on an asynchronously replicated (eventually consistent) database, what thought experiment reveals whether the application needs stronger guarantees?

options.text: Ask how the application behaves if replication lag grows to minutes or hours
Measure the average lag and set a service-level target at the p99
Assume replication is synchronous and handle the exceptions that arise
Test only under normal load, where lag is a fraction of a second

questions.explanation: Lag is normally brief but has no universal upper bound under overload or failure. Designing against a minutes-or-hours scenario reveals whether the application needs stronger routing, transactions, or explicit user feedback.

questions.question: In the context of replication lag and similar anomalies, why do database transactions exist?

options.text: So the database provides stronger guarantees and apps can be simpler
Mainly to increase write throughput by batching writes on the leader node
Mainly to shrink the replication log that the leader sends to followers
Mainly to let followers accept client writes directly, without a leader

questions.explanation: Working around replication issues in application code, for example by reading certain things from the leader, is complex and easy to get wrong. Transactions are a way for a database to provide stronger guarantees so that the application can be simpler and can trust the database to do the right thing. They typically cost throughput rather than increasing it, and they are not a log-compression or leaderless-write mechanism.

questions.question: Many distributed databases abandoned transactions, claiming they are too expensive and eventual consistency is inevitable. How should that claim be judged?

options.text: Partly true, but overly simplistic; stronger guarantees remain achievable at scale
Largely correct: beyond one node, coordination makes transactions impractical
Mostly wrong: transactions cost about the same in a cluster as on one node
Correct for multi-leader setups, but wrong for single-leader replication

questions.explanation: Coordination and transactions can be expensive or unavailable during partitions, but that does not make eventual consistency the only scalable design. Many systems provide stronger guarantees by narrowing transaction scope or accepting specific latency and availability costs.

questions.question: What is the main structural downside of leader-based replication?

options.text: There is only one leader, so if you cannot reach it you cannot write
Reads cannot be scaled out, because every read must also go to the leader
Conflicts must be resolved by the application, since two leaders may diverge
Followers cannot be added without taking the whole cluster down for a rebuild

questions.explanation: In leader-based replication all writes must go through the single leader, so if you cannot connect to it for any reason, such as a network interruption between you and the leader, you cannot write. Reads can be scaled with followers, conflict resolution is a multi-leader problem, and new followers can be added online from a snapshot. In a partitioned database each partition has its own leader, with the same limitation per partition.

questions.question: What defines a multi-leader replication configuration?

options.text: Several nodes accept writes, and each forwards its writes to all the others
One node accepts writes, and every other node serves reads only
A new leader is elected for each individual write request
Clients write directly to several replicas, with every node an equal peer

questions.explanation: Multi-leader replication (also called active/active) extends leader-based replication by allowing more than one node to accept writes. Each node that processes a write forwards the change to all other nodes, so each leader simultaneously acts as a follower to the other leaders. Because different leaders can accept concurrent writes to the same data, write conflicts become possible. One writer with read-only followers is single-leader, and clients writing to several replicas directly is leaderless.

questions.question: Does multi-leader replication usually make sense within a single datacenter?

options.text: Rarely; within one datacenter the added complexity outweighs the benefits
It is the recommended default configuration within a single datacenter
It is required in order to achieve high availability inside one datacenter
It cannot be configured within one datacenter, only between separate ones

questions.explanation: Within one datacenter the benefits of multiple leaders rarely outweigh the added complexity, chiefly write conflicts and subtle interactions with database features. It becomes reasonable when there is a real reason for several write-accepting locations, such as multiple datacenters, clients that work offline, or collaborative editing. It is not required for high availability, which single-leader failover can provide.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication across several datacenters, what is the typical architecture?

options.text: One leader per datacenter, replicating leader-to-leader between them
One global leader replicates to followers in all datacenters
All nodes in all datacenters are leaders with no followers
Each datacenter has followers only, with the leader outside

questions.explanation: Each datacenter has its own leader. Within a datacenter, regular leader-follower replication is used; between datacenters, each leader replicates its changes to the leaders in the other datacenters. This lets writes be processed locally, so a whole datacenter can fail or be far away without blocking writes elsewhere, at the cost of resolving conflicts between leaders.

questions.question: In a multi-datacenter deployment, which statements correctly compare multi-leader with single-leader replication? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Multi-leader processes writes in the local datacenter, hiding inter-datacenter latency
With multi-leader, each datacenter can keep operating during another's outage
Asynchronous multi-leader tolerates inter-datacenter network problems better
Single-leader needs conflict resolution, while multi-leader avoids conflicts by design

questions.explanation: In a single-leader setup every write must cross to the leader's datacenter, adding latency and making writes sensitive to the inter-datacenter link. With a leader per datacenter, writes are processed locally and replicated asynchronously, each datacenter can continue independently during another's outage, and temporary network interruptions do not stop writes. The claim about conflicts is reversed: multi-leader is the configuration that requires conflict resolution.

optionExplanations.a: A local leader acknowledges nearby writes without waiting for another datacenter, hiding wide-area latency from the normal write path.
optionExplanations.b: Because each datacenter has a write leader, one site can continue accepting local writes while another site is unavailable.
optionExplanations.c: Asynchronous links let each leader proceed through a temporary inter-datacenter partition and exchange changes after connectivity returns.
optionExplanations.d: Multi-leader replicas may accept concurrent writes to the same record, so conflicts are a central cost rather than something eliminated by disjoint ownership.

questions.question: Which external tools retrofit multi-leader replication onto a database? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Tungsten Replicator for MySQL
BDR for PostgreSQL
GoldenGate for Oracle
Bucardo for Cassandra

questions.explanation: Tungsten Replicator, BDR and GoldenGate can add cross-leader change propagation to their respective databases. Bucardo is associated with PostgreSQL rather than Cassandra.

optionExplanations.a: Tungsten Replicator can capture and forward MySQL changes between writable sites, retrofitting a multi-leader topology around the database.
optionExplanations.b: BDR was designed to provide bidirectional replication for PostgreSQL, allowing multiple PostgreSQL nodes to accept writes.
optionExplanations.c: Oracle GoldenGate transports database changes across systems and can be configured for active-active, multi-leader replication.
optionExplanations.d: Bucardo is a PostgreSQL replication tool, not a Cassandra retrofit; Cassandra already uses its own leaderless replication architecture.

questions.question: Multi-leader replication is often retrofitted onto databases designed around a single leader. What problem does this commonly cause?

options.text: Autoincrementing keys, triggers and integrity constraints can misbehave
It becomes slower than single-leader replication in essentially every workload
It can only run between nodes in one datacenter, never across datacenters
It requires fully synchronous replication between all of the leaders

questions.explanation: Features designed around one serialization point may make different decisions on different leaders: auto-incremented keys can collide, triggers can run repeatedly, and constraints may be satisfied locally but violated after replication.

questions.question: Which scenario is the offline-operation use case for multi-leader replication?

options.text: Each device's local calendar database accepts offline edits and syncs later
A read-only local cache on each device that synchronizes whenever connectivity returns
A single-leader setup in which each device runs a local read-only follower
A leaderless store in which each device performs quorum writes when online

questions.explanation: Treating each device as a local leader lets it accept calendar edits without a network connection. When connectivity returns, the device exchanges changes and resolves any concurrent edits.

questions.question: How does offline operation relate to multi-datacenter replication?

options.text: It is cross-datacenter multi-leader taken to the extreme: each device is a datacenter
The two are unrelated architectures that merely happen to share some vocabulary
Offline operation is really a form of leaderless replication with quorum reads
Offline operation is single-leader replication with a very long failover timeout

questions.explanation: A disconnected device accepts local writes and later exchanges them with other writable replicas, like a datacenter leader after a network interruption. Concurrent offline edits therefore need the same conflict rules.

questions.question: In real-time collaborative editing, what is the local replica?

options.text: A writable copy of the document in each collaborator's browser or client
None; the server holds the only replica and browsers are stateless views of it
A copy on the server that each collaborator must lock before editing
A read-only cache in the browser that is refreshed from the server

questions.explanation: When a user edits, the change is applied instantly to their local replica, the state of the document in their web browser or client application, and asynchronously replicated to the server and to other users editing the same document. Because each local replica accepts writes, collaborative editing has much in common with offline multi-leader replication, including the need for conflict resolution.

questions.question: In real-time collaborative editing, how can an application guarantee there will be no editing conflicts, and what replication model is that equivalent to?

options.text: Lock the document to one editor, equivalent to single-leader replication
It must use CRDTs, which is equivalent to leaderless replication
It must version every keystroke, which is equivalent to multi-leader replication
It must resolve conflicts on read, which is equivalent to quorum replication

questions.explanation: If the application obtains a lock on the document before a user can edit it, another user must wait until the first user has committed their changes and released the lock. Only one writer at a time means there is nothing concurrent to conflict, which is equivalent to single-leader replication with transactions on the leader. CRDTs, per-keystroke versions and on-read resolution handle conflicts rather than preventing them.

questions.question: In real-time collaborative editing, how can collaboration be made faster than with document locking, and what does that cost?
