options.text: Use tiny changes, like keystrokes, without locks; conflicts must then be resolved
Make each change larger and lock more often; the cost is higher editing latency
Send every change synchronously through a single leader; the cost is availability
Compress and batch changes before sending them; the cost is network bandwidth

questions.explanation: For faster collaboration you make the unit of change very small, such as a single keystroke, and avoid locking. Multiple users can then edit simultaneously, but the system inherits all the challenges of multi-leader replication, including conflict resolution. Larger changes, more locking or a single synchronous leader would slow collaboration rather than speed it up.

questions.question: Two users concurrently change a wiki page title from A to B and from A to C on different leaders. Trace the conflict.

options.text: Each leader accepts its own title; the conflict is found later, asynchronously
Both writes go through the same leader, so the second write is rejected outright
User 1's write is lost before reaching any leader, so only title C survives
The second leader detects the conflict at write time and blocks the second user

questions.explanation: Each user's change is applied successfully to their local leader, so both writes succeed. The conflict is detected only when the changes are replicated asynchronously and each leader receives a title that differs from its own; by then it may be too late to ask the user to resolve it. In a single-leader database the second writer would instead block or be aborted, and a multi-leader leader does not check other leaders at write time unless conflict detection is made synchronous, which would give up the main advantage of multiple leaders.

questions.question: When are write conflicts detected in single-leader versus multi-leader replication?

options.text: Immediately with one leader, but only after replication with multiple leaders
Both detect conflicts synchronously; the difference is only in resolution
Multi-leader detects conflicts synchronously and single-leader asynchronously
Conflicts go undetected in both setups, leaving the application to discover them when it next reads

questions.explanation: One leader serializes competing writes before acknowledging them, so it can reject a conflict immediately. Separate leaders accept locally and discover conflicts only when their asynchronous streams meet.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, how does assigning each user a home datacenter avoid write conflicts?

options.text: All writes for that user's records go through the leader in the home datacenter
Each write gets a timestamp, so the latest write wins in every datacenter
Every datacenter accepts every write, and the values are merged later
Only the user's reads, not writes, are routed to the home datacenter

questions.explanation: Assigning each record or user a home datacenter routes all of its writes through one leader. The wider deployment remains multi-leader, but each key receives single-leader ordering.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, conflict avoidance routes all writes for a record through one designated leader. When does it break down? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because one datacenter has failed and you need to reroute traffic to another datacenter
Because a user has moved to a different location and is now closer to a different datacenter
Because the record's schema changed between the two writes being applied
Because the replication topology had been reconfigured to all-to-all beforehand

questions.explanation: Conflict avoidance works only while each record has one designated leader. When you change that leader, for example because a datacenter failed and traffic is rerouted, or because a user moved closer to another datacenter, writes may arrive at both old and new leaders, and you have to deal with concurrent writes on different leaders.

optionExplanations.a: Failing over a user's writes to another datacenter temporarily removes the single home-leader rule, so the old and new sites may later contain concurrent updates.
optionExplanations.b: Reassigning a mobile user to a nearer datacenter changes the write authority and can overlap with updates still arriving through the former home site.
optionExplanations.c: Schema evolution can complicate replication, but it does not by itself make two leaders accept concurrent writes after a home-leader policy.
optionExplanations.d: An all-to-all propagation topology changes how writes travel, not which leader is authorized for a record, so it does not alone break conflict avoidance.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, a page title is concurrently changed from A to B on leader 1 and from A to C on leader 2. If each leader simply applies writes in the order it receives them, what is the result?

options.text: Leader 1 ends with C and leader 2 with B, so the replicas now disagree
Both leaders converge on B without any extra mechanism being needed
Leader 1 ends with B and leader 2 with C, and the earlier write is correct
Both leaders end with C, which is correct because it was written second

questions.explanation: Leader 1 applies its local B and then the replicated C; leader 2 applies its local C and then the replicated B. Neither order is more correct, and simply applying writes in arrival order leaves C at leader 1 and B at leader 2. That is unacceptable, because every replication scheme must ensure all replicas eventually hold the same data, so conflicts must be resolved convergently. A single-leader database avoids this by applying writes in one sequential order.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, which approaches achieve convergent conflict resolution? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Highest ID wins — give each write a unique ID such as a timestamp, long random number, UUID, or hash of the key and value, pick the write with the highest ID as the winner and throw away the other writes. If a timestamp is used, this is known as last write wins (LWW); although popular, it is dangerously prone to data loss
Highest replica number wins — give each replica a unique ID and let writes that originated at a higher-numbered replica always take precedence; this approach also implies data loss
Merge the values together — for example order them alphabetically and then concatenate them, so the merged title might be 'B/C'
Roll both writes back and return an error to each client, so that both users retry against whichever leader wins the election

questions.explanation: Convergence requires every replica to resolve the same conflict identically. Deterministic winners and deterministic merges do that, while recording all conflicting values defers resolution without discarding information. Rolling back both independently accepted writes is not a normal convergent strategy; winner-based methods such as LWW can silently lose data.

optionExplanations.a: A globally deterministic write ID makes every replica select the same winner, so states converge, although discarding the losing values can silently lose valid updates.
optionExplanations.b: A fixed replica-ID priority also makes every node choose identically, but origin priority is arbitrary and loses writes from lower-ranked replicas.
optionExplanations.c: A deterministic merge function incorporates both values and produces the same result everywhere, preserving more information than a winner-takes-all rule.
optionExplanations.d: Once separate leaders have acknowledged writes independently, rolling both back through a later leader election is neither reliably coordinated nor a standard convergent merge rule.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, custom conflict-resolution code can run on write or on read. How do these differ?

options.text: On write, a fast background handler resolves it; on read, all versions go to the app
On write, the handler prompts the user at once; on read, the database keeps only the newest
On write, all conflicting versions are stored; on read, a background handler picks one quickly
On write, the conflicting write is rejected to the client; on read, the replicas re-run it

questions.explanation: On write, as soon as the database detects a conflict in the log of replicated changes, it calls a handler (Bucardo, for example, accepts a Perl snippet); it runs in a background process, must execute quickly and typically cannot prompt a user. On read, all conflicting writes are stored, and the next read returns the multiple versions to the application, which may prompt the user or resolve automatically and write the result back; CouchDB works this way. The roles are not reversed, an on-write handler cannot wait for a user, and neither mode rejects the write, since in multi-leader replication both writes have already succeeded on their own leaders.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, at what granularity does conflict resolution usually apply?

options.text: At the level of an individual row or document, not a whole transaction
At the level of an entire transaction, which is resolved atomically
At the level of an entire table, which is resolved as a single unit
At the level of the whole database, which is resolved at failover time

questions.explanation: Replicas commonly resolve each conflicting row or document independently. A transaction that changed several objects can therefore be broken apart during conflict resolution, even if it committed atomically at one leader.

questions.question: In a frequently cited Amazon example, what went wrong with the shopping cart's conflict-resolution handler?

options.text: Amazon's shopping cart kept added items but lost removals
Amazon lost entire carts during a datacenter failover
Amazon's handler merged carts across different customers
Amazon's handler always picked the newest cart, discarding older items

questions.explanation: For some time the conflict-resolution logic on Amazon's shopping cart preserved items added to the cart but not items removed from it, so customers sometimes saw previously removed items reappear. Merging by keeping all additions is easy; correctly preserving removals requires recording deletions explicitly, for example with tombstones. It shows how custom resolution code can be error-prone.

questions.question: Which lines of research aim to resolve conflicts from concurrent data modifications automatically? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Conflict-free replicated datatypes (CRDTs) — a family of data structures for sets, maps, ordered lists, counters and so on that can be concurrently edited by multiple users and automatically resolve conflicts in sensible ways; some have been implemented in Riak 2.0
Mergeable persistent data structures — which track history explicitly, similarly to the Git version control system, and use a three-way merge function, whereas CRDTs use two-way merges

Operational transformation — the conflict resolution algorithm behind collaborative editing applications such as Etherpad and Google Docs, designed particularly for concurrent editing of an ordered list of items, such as the list of characters that constitute a text document
Byzantine fault-tolerant merging — the approach taken by blockchain databases, where individual replicas cannot be trusted to report their own state honestly

questions.explanation: CRDTs are data structures such as sets, maps, lists and counters that merge concurrent edits automatically; mergeable persistent data structures track history like Git and use three-way merges; operational transformation transforms concurrent edits to an ordered list such as text. At the time of writing their database implementations were young, but automatic conflict resolution could make multi-leader synchronization much simpler for applications. Byzantine fault tolerance addresses untrustworthy nodes, not ordinary merges.

optionExplanations.a: CRDTs define data-type-specific merge behavior that is associative and convergent, allowing replicas to reconcile concurrent set, map, list or counter edits automatically.
optionExplanations.b: Mergeable persistent structures retain ancestry so a three-way merge can compare two descendants with their common base, much like version-control systems.
optionExplanations.c: Operational transformation rewrites concurrent ordered-list edits relative to one another and has been used for collaborative text editing.
optionExplanations.d: Byzantine consensus addresses dishonest or arbitrary participants, not the ordinary concurrent-update merge problem these three research lines target.

questions.question: A multi-leader room-booking system checks a room's availability before confirming each reservation. Why can two bookings still conflict?

options.text: Each leader's check passes locally, so both overlapping bookings confirm
The check holds, so conflicts arise only if a leader fails over mid-booking
The check fails because the clocks on the two leaders are not synchronized
The check is unnecessary, because rooms are partitioned across the leaders

questions.explanation: Each leader evaluates availability against only its local state, so both checks can pass before replication reveals the overlap. Preventing this invariant violation requires coordination or a serializable conflict-detection scheme.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, what is a replication topology?

options.text: The communication paths along which writes propagate from one node to another
The physical cabling and switch layout of the datacenter network
The assignment of key ranges to partitions across the nodes
The order in which a conflict handler applies concurrent writes

questions.explanation: A topology describes the directed paths over which leaders forward writes. With two leaders the useful arrangement is simply bidirectional; rings, stars and all-to-all choices appear with three or more.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication with more than two leaders, which topology is the most general, and which did MySQL support by default at the time of writing?

options.text: All-to-all is most general; MySQL by default supported only circular
Circular is the most general; MySQL by default supported only all-to-all
Star is the most general; MySQL by default supported only a star topology
Tree is the most general; MySQL by default supported only a tree topology

questions.explanation: In all-to-all every leader sends its writes to every other leader, which is the most general topology. More restricted topologies are also used: MySQL by default supported only a circular topology, in which each node receives writes from one node and forwards them, plus its own, to one other node. In a star, one root node forwards writes to all others, and a star can be generalized to a tree. A replication star is unrelated to an analytics star schema.

questions.question: In multi-leader circular and star replication topologies, how does a node recognize a change it has already processed, so that writes do not loop forever?

options.text: Each write is tagged with the identifier of every node it has passed through
A time-to-live counter attached to every write, decremented at each hop
A global sequence number assigned to each write by the root node of the topology
A lock held on the record for as long as the write circulates around the ring

questions.explanation: In circular and star topologies a write may pass through several nodes before reaching all replicas, so nodes must forward changes they receive from others, which could loop forever. To prevent this, each node has a unique identifier, and each write in the replication log is tagged with the identifiers of every node it has passed through. A node that receives a change tagged with its own identifier ignores it, because it has already processed that change.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication, how does the fault tolerance of circular and star topologies compare with all-to-all?

options.text: Circular and star are worse: one failed node can cut off replication for others
All-to-all is the least fault tolerant, because it has the most links that can fail
All three topologies tolerate a single node failure equally well in practice
Star is the most fault tolerant, because the root node can itself be replicated

questions.explanation: In circular and star topologies, if just one node fails it can interrupt the flow of replication messages between other nodes until it is fixed, and reconfiguring around it is usually manual. All-to-all lets messages travel along different paths, avoiding a single point of failure, so its fault tolerance is better. Its own weakness is different: messages on faster links can overtake others.

questions.question: In an all-to-all multi-leader topology, client A inserts a row on leader 1, and client B then updates that row on leader 3. What can go wrong at leader 2?

options.text: Leader 2 may receive B's update before A's insert, which it depends on
Client A and client B both insert the same row, which causes a duplicate key error
Leader 2 crashes before either write reaches it, so both of the writes are lost
The two writes conflict directly and have to be merged by the application

questions.explanation: Because network links have different speeds, replication messages can overtake one another. Leader 2 may receive B's update first, which from its point of view is an update to a row that does not exist, and only later the insert that should have preceded it. This is a problem of causality: the update depends on the insert, so every node must process the insert first.

questions.question: If a dependent update reaches a multi-leader replica before the insert it modifies, why can't wall-clock timestamps reliably restore causal order, and what technique can?

options.text: Clocks can't be trusted to be in sync; version vectors can order them
Timestamps do solve it, provided every node runs NTP against the same source
Timestamps fail only because they are too coarse; sequence numbers solve it
The anomaly cannot be fixed by any technique, so it must simply be tolerated

questions.explanation: Attaching a wall-clock timestamp to each write is not enough, because clocks cannot be trusted to be sufficiently in sync to order these events correctly at the receiving leader. Version vectors track causal dependencies logically, by counting writes per replica, so a node can tell that the update depends on an insert it has not yet seen. Finer timestamps do not fix clock skew, and the problem is solvable.

questions.question: At the time of writing, how did PostgreSQL BDR and Tungsten Replicator for MySQL fall short in handling multi-leader conflicts?

options.text: BDR did not provide causal ordering of writes; Tungsten did not even try to detect conflicts
BDR duplicated every write on each leader; Tungsten silently dropped concurrent writes
Both lacked support for circular replication topologies of any kind
Both could be deployed only within a single datacenter, not across several

questions.explanation: Conflict detection and causal ordering are poorly implemented in many multi-leader systems. At the time of writing, PostgreSQL BDR did not provide causal ordering of writes, so dependent updates could be applied out of order, and Tungsten Replicator for MySQL did not even try to detect conflicts. Both are multi-datacenter tools, which is why their conflict handling matters.

questions.question: Because conflict detection and write ordering are poorly implemented in many multi-leader systems, what should you do when using one? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Be aware of the conflict and write-ordering issues it can have
Read its documentation carefully to learn its actual guarantees
Thoroughly test it to ensure it provides the guarantees you believe it has
Disable its conflict resolution and leave all conflicts to the application

questions.explanation: Multi-leader systems vary widely in how they detect conflicts and order writes, and some do neither well. So you should be aware of these issues, read the documentation carefully, and thoroughly test the database to check it really provides the guarantees you assume. Disabling conflict resolution does not remove conflicts; it leaves divergent values for the application to handle without a strategy.

optionExplanations.a: Multi-leader behavior includes subtle conflict, ordering and topology failure modes, so operators must explicitly account for them rather than treating replication as transparent.
optionExplanations.b: Product-specific documentation defines conflict detection, resolution and durability behavior that cannot be inferred merely from the label multi-leader.
optionExplanations.c: Fault and concurrency testing checks whether the implementation actually preserves the guarantees the application assumes under realistic failures.
optionExplanations.d: Disabling resolution does not remove conflicts; it leaves divergent values or shifts unresolved state to the application without a complete strategy.

questions.question: What do single-leader and multi-leader replication have in common, and what does leaderless replication abandon?

options.text: A leader orders all writes in both; leaderless lets any replica accept writes
Both use quorums to order writes; leaderless replication abandons quorums
Both are fully synchronous; leaderless replication is always asynchronous
Both rely on conflict resolution; leaderless replication avoids conflicts entirely

questions.explanation: In single-leader and multi-leader replication, a client sends each write to one node, a leader, which determines the order in which writes are processed, and followers apply them in that order. Leaderless replication abandons the leader and allows any replica to accept writes directly from clients, so no node imposes a write order. Quorums belong to leaderless systems, and leaderless systems still face conflicts.

questions.question: How did leaderless replication come to be a widely used architecture?

options.text: Early systems were leaderless; Amazon's Dynamo made it fashionable again
It was invented outright by Amazon in 2007 and had no earlier predecessors
It originated with Cassandra and was only later adopted by Amazon for Dynamo
It has always been the dominant architecture, even during the relational era

questions.explanation: Leaderless replication predates Amazon, but Dynamo revived interest in the design. Dynamo was an internal Amazon system; the hosted DynamoDB product has a different architecture and uses leaders internally.

questions.question: Which open source datastores have leaderless replication models inspired by Dynamo? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Riak
Cassandra
Voldemort
MongoDB

questions.explanation: Riak, Cassandra and Voldemort adopted leaderless ideas popularized by Dynamo, so they are often called Dynamo-style systems. MongoDB instead uses leader-based replication.

optionExplanations.a: Riak uses Dynamo-inspired leaderless requests, configurable quorums and version-based reconciliation rather than routing all writes through one leader.
optionExplanations.b: Cassandra combines Dynamo-style partitioning and quorum replication with ideas from Bigtable, allowing writes without a single per-key leader.
optionExplanations.c: Voldemort was explicitly inspired by Dynamo and uses a leaderless, partitioned key-value architecture with replica quorums.
optionExplanations.d: MongoDB replica sets elect a primary that accepts writes, so its normal replication model is leader-based rather than Dynamo-style leaderless.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, who sends a client's write to the replicas, and why is that node not a leader?

options.text: The client or a coordinator, but the coordinator imposes no write order
A coordinator node that behaves exactly like a leader, enforcing a write order
The replicas gossip among themselves, and clients never write to them directly
A leader elected at random for the duration of each individual write request

questions.explanation: In some leaderless implementations the client sends its writes directly to several replicas; in others a coordinator node does this on the client's behalf. Unlike a leader, the coordinator does not enforce a particular ordering of writes, so concurrent writes can reach replicas in different orders. That difference has major consequences, such as the need to detect and resolve concurrent writes.

questions.question: In a leaderless database with three replicas, one replica is down, and a write counts as successful once two replicas acknowledge it. What happens when a client writes?

options.text: The client writes to all three; two acknowledge and the third simply misses it
The write fails outright, because one of the three replicas is unavailable
The client blocks until all three replicas have acknowledged the write
A failover promotes a new leader first, after which the write proceeds normally

questions.explanation: A quorum write does not require every replica to respond. With three replicas and w = 2, acknowledgements from the two reachable replicas are sufficient; the missed replica can catch up later through repair.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, how does read repair fix a replica that missed writes while it was unavailable?

options.text: A client reading several replicas spots a stale version and writes the newer value back
The returning node is wiped and rebuilt from a snapshot of a healthy replica
The returning node is permanently excluded from serving any read requests
Clients read only from whichever node reports the longest current uptime

questions.explanation: A leaderless client sends reads to several replicas in parallel and uses version numbers to decide which response is newer. When it sees that one replica returned an older version, it writes the newer value back to that replica. This repairs staleness without a leader, but only for values that are actually read.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, for which values does read repair work well, and why?

options.text: Frequently read values, because repair happens only when a value is read
Rarely read values, because they are repaired by a background scan
Write-heavy values, because every write triggers a repair of all replicas
All values equally, because the server repairs every replica on a schedule

questions.explanation: Read repair happens only when a client reads a value from several replicas and notices a stale response, so frequently read values are repaired quickly. Values that are rarely read may stay missing or stale on some replicas, reducing their durability. Covering those requires a separate anti-entropy process that scans for differences in the background.

questions.question: In Dynamo-style leaderless datastores, what does a background anti-entropy process do?

options.text: It constantly compares replicas and copies missing data from one to another
It replays writes to stale replicas in the order they were originally made
It is read repair performed at write time instead of at read time
It reduces durability, because it deletes any value that has not been read

questions.explanation: An anti-entropy process runs in the background, looks for differences in the data between replicas and copies missing data across. Unlike a leader's replication log, it does not copy writes in any particular order, and there may be a significant delay before data is copied. Not every system has one (Voldemort did not at the time of writing); without it, rarely read values can stay stale indefinitely.

questions.question: In a leaderless database with three replicas, every successful write is guaranteed to be on at least two of them. Why does reading from any two replicas ensure at least one up-to-date value?

options.text: At most one replica can be stale, so any two replicas must include an up-to-date one
Results from two replicas are averaged, which smooths out any stale value
The two replicas read are always the same two that accepted the write
The third replica is always the stale one, and reading two avoids it

questions.explanation: If a write reaches two of three replicas, at most one can miss it. Reading from any two must therefore include at least one replica holding the new value; version metadata identifies that value.

questions.question: In a leaderless database with n replicas, each write must be confirmed by w nodes and each read queries r nodes. What condition makes reads expect an up-to-date value, and why?

options.text: w + r greater than n, so every read set overlaps every write set
w + r less than n, so reads and writes never compete for the same nodes
w equal to r, so reads and writes are symmetric whatever n is
w greater than r, so writes always reach more nodes than reads

questions.explanation: If every successful write is on at least w of the n replicas and every read contacts r replicas, then when w + r is greater than n the two sets cannot be disjoint: they must share at least one node, and that node has the latest value (version numbers identify which response is newest). For example, with n = 3, w = 2 and r = 2, a write misses at most one replica and any two replicas read include one that has it. If w + r is at most n, a read can land entirely on replicas that missed the write. Equal or unequal w and r does not matter by itself; only the sum relative to n does.

questions.question: What is the common choice of n, w and r in Dynamo-style databases, and what are the values for n = 3 and n = 5?

options.text: Odd n with majority quorums w = r = (n + 1) / 2: 2 for n = 3, 3 for n = 5
Make n even and set w and r each to n / 2, giving two apiece when n is four
Always set w equal to n and r equal to 1, whatever the number of replicas
Always set w equal to 1 and r equal to n, whatever the number of replicas

questions.explanation: For odd n, two simple majorities necessarily overlap: 2 of 3 or 3 of 5. The cluster itself may contain more than n machines; n is the number of replicas for one key, which also allows data to be partitioned.

questions.question: In a leaderless database with n replicas and a workload of few writes and many reads, which quorum setting fits, and what is its disadvantage?

options.text: Set w = n and r = 1: fast reads, but one failed node fails all writes
Set w = 1 and r = n, which speeds up writes with no disadvantage
Set w = r = 1, which maximizes availability with no risk of stale reads
Set w = r = n, which guarantees consistency at no cost

questions.explanation: With w = n every write reaches all replicas, so reading any single replica (r = 1) returns the latest value, and w + r = n + 1 still exceeds n. Reads become fast, but a write needs every replica to respond, so just one failed node causes all writes to fail. w = 1 with r = n favors writes instead, w = r = 1 breaks the quorum condition, and w = r = n makes both reads and writes fragile.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, which statements about how the quorum condition tolerates unavailable nodes are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If w is less than n, we can still process writes if a node is unavailable; if r is less than n, we can still process reads if a node is unavailable
With n = 3, w = 2, r = 2 we can tolerate one unavailable node; with n = 5, w = 3, r = 3 we can tolerate two unavailable nodes

Normally reads and writes are always sent to all n replicas in parallel — w and r determine how many nodes we wait for, that is, how many of the n nodes need to report success before we consider the read or write to be successful
Reads and writes are sent only to w or to r nodes respectively, chosen at random from the n home nodes responsible for that particular key

questions.explanation: If w is less than n, writes can proceed with a node unavailable; if r is less than n, reads can. With n = 3 and w = r = 2 one node can be down, and with n = 5 and w = r = 3 two can. Reads and writes are normally sent to all n replicas in parallel; w and r specify how many successful responses to wait for, not how many nodes to contact.

optionExplanations.a: When w or r is below n, an operation can succeed without every replica responding, so one unavailable node need not stop reads or writes.
optionExplanations.b: The stated quorums need responses from one fewer than all replicas: two of three tolerates one outage, while three of five tolerates two.
optionExplanations.c: Coordinators normally contact all home replicas to reduce latency and aid repair, then return after the configured number of successful responses arrives.
optionExplanations.d: Restricting sends to only w or r randomly chosen replicas would unnecessarily reduce repair opportunities; those symbols specify completion thresholds, not fan-out.

questions.question: In a leaderless database using strict quorums (no sloppy quorum), what happens if fewer than w or r nodes are available, and does the reason for unavailability matter?

options.text: The operation simply returns an error, whatever the underlying cause
The operation blocks until enough nodes return; the reason determines the retry policy
The operation succeeds with a warning; only crashes count as unavailable
The coordinator substitutes another node automatically; the reason is logged

questions.explanation: The coordinator only counts usable responses. Whether missing responses come from crashes, network loss or overload does not change the quorum test: fewer than w acknowledgements or r reads means failure.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, why are w and r often chosen to be majorities of n, and must a quorum always be a majority?

options.text: Majorities overlap and still tolerate a minority failing; other overlapping sets also work
Majorities are needed for overlap; a small w with a large r cannot overlap
Majorities minimize latency; non-majority quorums are always slower in practice
Majorities guarantee strong consistency; any other choice of w and r gives no guarantee at all

questions.explanation: If both w and r are majorities (more than n/2), their sum must exceed n, so every read set overlaps every write set, and operations still succeed while a minority of nodes is down (with n = 5 and w = r = 3, two nodes can be down). But quorums need not be majorities: all that matters is that the read and write sets overlap in at least one node, so other assignments, such as a small write quorum with a large read quorum, also work. Majorities are not about latency, and no choice of w and r gives an absolute strong-consistency guarantee because of edge cases such as sloppy quorums and concurrent writes.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, what happens if you deliberately set w + r to be less than or equal to n?

options.text: Fewer successful responses are needed, so stale reads become likelier
The database rejects the configuration outright as an invalid quorum setting
Reads remain guaranteed fresh, but acknowledged writes may silently be lost
Latency increases and availability decreases, which is why it is discouraged

questions.explanation: If w + r is at most n, a read set can be disjoint from the replicas that accepted the latest write. Fewer responses improve latency and availability, but reads may return stale values.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, stale values can be returned even when w + r is greater than n. In which scenarios? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A sloppy quorum may place the write on different nodes from those the read contacts
Concurrent writes, or a write concurrent with a read, may leave no single latest value
A write that failed overall may remain on the replicas where it succeeded
Reads are sent to all n replicas in parallel rather than to only r of them

questions.explanation: The inequality w plus r greater than n guarantees overlap only for the intended replica set under ordinary completed writes. Sloppy quorums can use different nodes, concurrent writes have no single latest value, partial writes are not rolled back, and restoring an old replica can reduce the number carrying a newer value.

optionExplanations.a: A sloppy write may reside on temporary substitute nodes while a later read contacts only the home replicas, so the usual read/write intersection does not apply.
optionExplanations.b: Concurrent writes create multiple incomparable current versions; quorum overlap cannot manufacture one unambiguous latest value without version reconciliation.
optionExplanations.c: A write that fails to reach w replicas may still leave a newer value on some nodes, and later reads can encounter either that value or older replicas.
optionExplanations.d: Sending reads to all n replicas is the normal behavior and, if anything, raises the chance of reaching an up-to-date replica; it does not cause stale results.

questions.question: In Dynamo-style leaderless databases, what do the quorum parameters w and r actually provide?

options.text: They tune the likelihood of stale reads; they do not guarantee freshness
They guarantee fresh reads whenever w + r is greater than n
They also provide monotonic reads and read-your-writes once w + r exceeds n
Quorums provide no guarantee of any kind, so w and r are merely advisory

questions.explanation: Choosing w + r greater than n makes read and write sets overlap, but edge cases such as sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, partially failed writes, restored replicas and unlucky timing can still return stale values. So w and r let you adjust the probability of reading stale values rather than giving absolute guarantees. They also usually do not provide read-your-writes, monotonic reads or consistent prefix reads; stronger guarantees generally require transactions or consensus.

questions.question: How do you compute replication lag in a leader-based system, and what makes the computation possible?

options.text: Each node's position in the replication log, subtracted from the leader's
By comparing each follower's current wall-clock time with the leader's
By counting the rows on each node and taking the difference between totals
It cannot be measured directly at all, only estimated from query latencies

questions.explanation: A single ordered log gives every node a scalar position, which is what makes subtraction meaningful. If a follower falls behind significantly the monitoring should alert you, which may indicate a problem in the network or an overloaded node.

questions.question: Why is measuring replication staleness harder in a leaderless database than in a leader-based one? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because in leaderless replication there is no fixed order in which writes are applied, so there is no single log position to compare
Because if the database only uses read repair with no anti-entropy process, there is no limit to how old a value might be — a value that is infrequently read may be ancient
Because leaderless databases maintain no version numbers for their stored values, so there is nothing to compare
Because a client cannot read from more than one replica per request, so it never sees the divergence at all

questions.explanation: A leader's ordered log gives followers comparable progress positions. Leaderless replicas lack one universal order, and read repair alone may leave rarely read values stale indefinitely. Probabilistic models can estimate stale-read rates from n, w and r, but such monitoring is not yet common practice.

optionExplanations.a: Without one leader log, replicas can receive concurrent writes in different orders, so there is no single offset that measures every replica's lag.
optionExplanations.b: Read repair touches only keys that clients read; an infrequently accessed key can therefore remain arbitrarily old without an anti-entropy process.
optionExplanations.c: Leaderless databases do store version metadata such as timestamps or version vectors; the difficulty is the lack of one globally ordered progress position.
optionExplanations.d: Quorum reads commonly contact several replicas precisely to compare versions, so single-replica visibility is not the reason staleness is hard to monitor.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, which benefits do appropriately configured quorums provide? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They let a database tolerate the failure of individual nodes without the need for failover
They tolerate individual nodes going slow, because requests don't have to wait for all n nodes to respond — they can return when w or r nodes have responded
They suit use cases that require high availability and low latency, and that can tolerate occasional stale reads
They guarantee that no stale value is ever returned to a client, under every possible failure scenario

questions.explanation: Because any w or r replicas suffice, a leaderless database can tolerate individual node failures without failover and individual slow nodes without waiting for them. That makes it appealing for use cases needing high availability and low latency that can tolerate occasional stale reads. It does not eliminate staleness, because of edge cases such as sloppy quorums and concurrent writes.

optionExplanations.a: Any replica can participate and the coordinator waits for a quorum, so an individual failure does not require promoting a replacement leader before operations continue.
optionExplanations.b: The request returns after w or r responses rather than waiting for all n replicas, preventing one slow node from determining normal latency.
optionExplanations.c: This partial-response design favors availability and latency, but applications must tolerate stale or conflicting versions in the edge cases quorum overlap does not cover.
optionExplanations.d: Quorum inequalities do not eliminate staleness under sloppy placement, concurrent writes, failed writes or restored old replicas, so an absolute freshness guarantee is false.

questions.question: In a leaderless database, what situation motivates sloppy quorums?

options.text: Home nodes are alive but a network interruption cuts the client off from them
Every node in the cluster has crashed at once, so no quorum can be formed at all
Two clients write the same key concurrently, so their values must be merged
The node clocks have drifted apart, so writes can no longer be ordered

questions.explanation: A network interruption can cut a client off from many database nodes. Those nodes are alive, and other clients may reach them, but to this client they might as well be dead, so it may not reach w or r of the value's n home nodes. In a large cluster it can still reach other nodes, and a sloppy quorum accepts the write on those reachable substitute nodes rather than returning an error. If every node had crashed there would be nothing to write to, concurrent writes are a conflict-resolution problem, and clock drift is unrelated.

questions.question: In leaderless replication, what are a sloppy quorum and hinted handoff?

options.text: A sloppy quorum counts reachable non-home nodes toward w or r; hinted handoff sends writes home
A sloppy quorum lowers w and r below the quorum threshold; hinted handoff retries failed writes
A sloppy quorum writes to fewer than w nodes; hinted handoff is the background anti-entropy scan
A sloppy quorum elects a temporary leader; hinted handoff demotes it once the network heals

questions.explanation: A sloppy quorum still seeks w or r responses, but it may count temporary non-home nodes when the normal replicas are unreachable. Hinted handoff later transfers those temporary copies to their intended owners.

questions.question: Why is a sloppy quorum not really a quorum in the traditional sense, even when w + r is greater than n?

options.text: Because it raises write availability but breaks the read-freshness guarantee
Because it contacts fewer than w nodes, so writes are not durable at all
Because it does not actually increase availability for writes in any way
Because it guarantees only freshness of reads, and never durability of writes

questions.explanation: Substitute nodes can durably store the write, but a later read may contact only the unreachable home replicas and miss it. Thus the response counts no longer guarantee write/read overlap or freshness.

questions.question: In common Dynamo-style implementations (at the time of writing), are sloppy quorums optional, and what are the defaults?

options.text: Optional everywhere: default on in Riak, off in Cassandra and Voldemort
They are mandatory in all three of Riak, Cassandra and Voldemort
They are enabled by default in all three of those implementations
They are disabled by default in all three of those implementations

questions.explanation: Common Dynamo-style implementations make sloppy quorums configurable rather than mandatory. Riak enables them by default, whereas Cassandra and Voldemort default to using only the designated home replicas.

questions.question: How do Cassandra and Voldemort handle multi-datacenter operation?

options.text: n spans all datacenters, but the client waits only for a quorum in its local datacenter
They keep all communication local to one datacenter and replicate asynchronously between clusters
They require a write quorum spanning every datacenter before acknowledging a write
They elect one leader per datacenter, as in multi-leader replication

questions.explanation: Cassandra and Voldemort keep multi-datacenter support within the normal leaderless model: the n replicas include nodes in all datacenters, configuration states how many replicas each datacenter holds, and each write is sent to all of them, but the client usually waits only for a quorum within its local datacenter, so cross-datacenter delays and interruptions do not affect it. Writes to remote datacenters are often asynchronous. Riak instead keeps client traffic within one datacenter, with n counting replicas there, and replicates between clusters asynchronously, much like multi-leader replication.

questions.question: In Dynamo-style leaderless databases, conflicts can occur even with strict quorums. Besides concurrent client writes, on which occasions can they arise?

options.text: During read repair or hinted handoff
During compaction or snapshotting
During failover or leader election
When a quorum read gets the same version back from every replica it contacts

questions.explanation: Dynamo-style databases let several clients write the same key concurrently, so conflicts occur as in multi-leader replication. They can also arise during read repair and hinted handoff, because both copy values between nodes outside the normal client write path, and those values may race with other writes. There is no failover or leader election in a leaderless system, compaction and snapshots do not create concurrent versions, and identical versions from every replica mean there is nothing to reconcile.

questions.question: In a three-node leaderless datastore, clients A and B concurrently write key X. Node 1 receives only A's write; node 2 receives A then B; node 3 receives B then A. If each node simply overwrites the value whenever it receives a write, what is the final state?

options.text: Node 2 holds B, nodes 1 and 3 hold A, and they stay inconsistent forever
All three nodes converge on B, since it was the last write sent to the cluster
All three nodes converge on A, since a majority of nodes received A first
A coordinator serializes the writes, so all three nodes end up agreeing

questions.explanation: Each node keeps whichever write arrived last: node 1 only saw A, node 2 saw B last, and node 3 saw A last. So node 2 thinks X is B while the others think it is A, and nothing will ever reconcile them. Because neither client knew of the other's write, the writes are concurrent and have no natural order; to become eventually consistent, the replicas need a rule for converging on the same value, not per-node arrival order. Leaderless coordinators do not impose an order.

questions.question: In Dynamo-style databases, how well do implementations handle concurrent-write conflicts, and what does that oblige application developers to do?

options.text: Most handle them poorly; developers must understand the database's conflict handling
Most handle them well; developers can rely on automatic convergence without losing data
They are resolved by consensus; developers only need to retry writes that time out
They are never detected; developers must prevent concurrent writes by locking each key

questions.explanation: One might hope replicated databases converge automatically, but most implementations are quite poor at it. If you want to avoid losing data, you, the application developer, need to know a lot about the internals of your database's conflict handling, such as whether it uses last write wins or returns siblings for you to merge. Dynamo-style databases do not run consensus on each write, they do detect concurrency (for example with version numbers), and they do not offer per-key locks; the work lies in choosing and implementing a merge policy.

questions.question: In leaderless replication, how does last write wins (LWW) resolve concurrent values?

options.text: Keep the value with the greatest timestamp and discard the rest
Merge all concurrent values into one combined value
Keep the value with the smallest timestamp, since it came first
Store all concurrent values as siblings for the client to merge

questions.explanation: Concurrent writes have no natural order, so LWW forces an arbitrary one: attach a timestamp to each write, treat the biggest timestamp as the most recent, and discard writes with earlier timestamps. At the time of writing it was the only conflict resolution method supported in Cassandra and an optional feature in Riak. It achieves convergence but may silently discard writes that were acknowledged. Merging and keeping siblings are the alternatives that preserve data.

questions.question: What does last write wins (LWW) cost in exchange for eventual convergence?

options.text: Concurrent acknowledged writes are silently lost, and clock skew can drop others too
Only writes that were genuinely concurrent with one another are ever discarded
No write is ever discarded; writes are merely reordered by their timestamps
Nothing, because convergence comes for free with a timestamp comparison

questions.explanation: LWW converges at the cost of durability: if several writes to the same key are concurrent, even if all were reported successful because they reached w replicas, only one survives and the others are silently discarded. Because it relies on timestamps from unreliable clocks, LWW can even drop writes that were not concurrent. It is acceptable only where lost writes are tolerable, such as caching.

questions.question: What is the only safe way to use a database with LWW?

options.text: Write each key only once and treat it as immutable, e.g. by using a UUID key
Synchronize every clock with NTP and rely on wall-clock timestamps instead
Apply last-write-wins to reads only, and resolve write conflicts in the app
Set w equal to n, so that every replica agrees before a write is accepted

questions.explanation: LWW can discard concurrent writes to the same key. Giving every write a fresh immutable key, such as a UUID, prevents two writes from competing for that key and removes the destructive conflict.

questions.question: What makes one operation happen before another in a distributed system, and when are two operations concurrent?

options.text: A precedes B if B knows of, depends on or builds on A; if neither, they are concurrent
A happens before B if A's timestamp is smaller; concurrency means equal timestamps
A happens before B if A was sent from a lower-numbered node; concurrency means same node
A happens before B whenever A committed first, so true concurrency cannot arise

questions.explanation: Causality is based on information flow, not wall-clock timestamps. If B observed or depended on A, then A happened before B; if neither operation could know about the other, they are concurrent.

questions.question: Consider two pairs of writes: (1) client A inserts a row, and client B then increments the value A inserted; (2) two clients each write the same key, each unaware of the other. Which pair is concurrent?

options.text: The increment pair is causal; the mutually unaware pair is the concurrent one
The increment pair is the concurrent one; the mutually unaware pair is causal
Both pairs are concurrent, since neither operation builds on the other one
Both pairs are causally dependent, so concurrency arises in neither of them

questions.explanation: An increment derived from an inserted value depends on that insert, so the operations are causally ordered. When neither client has observed the other's write, neither operation happens before the other and they are concurrent.

questions.question: Must two operations overlap in time for a replicated system to treat them as concurrent?

options.text: No; concurrency means neither operation knew about the other, not overlap in time
Yes; concurrency is defined purely by overlapping intervals on a wall clock
No; relativity makes concurrency undefinable, so systems ignore it
Yes; the speed of light sets the minimum time window for concurrency

questions.explanation: Two operations are concurrent if both are unaware of each other, regardless of the physical time at which they occurred. Exact time is hard to determine in distributed systems anyway because clocks are unreliable. The relativity analogy explains why distant events cannot affect each other, but computer systems are broader: two operations far apart in time can still be concurrent if network problems prevented one from learning about the other.

questions.question: A server keeps one version number per key and returns all non-overwritten values on each read. Client 1 writes [milk] (version 1). Client 2, unaware of it, writes [eggs] (version 2), and the server keeps both values. Client 1 then writes [milk, flour], sending version 1 from its last read. What does the server now store?

options.text: [milk, flour] replaces [milk] but is kept alongside the concurrent [eggs]
Only [milk, flour], because it is the newest write the server has received
Nothing new; it rejects the write because version 1 is already out of date
[milk], [eggs] and [milk, flour], all kept as siblings to be merged later

questions.explanation: The version number tells the server which prior state the client observed. The new value supersedes that ancestor, while the unseen [eggs] branch remains a concurrent sibling that must be merged rather than overwritten.

questions.question: In a version-number scheme for a shopping cart, two clients repeatedly write concurrently, each sending the version from its last read. What does a graph of which writes depended on which reveal?

options.text: No client is ever fully current, yet old versions get overwritten and nothing is lost
The server serialized every write, so none of them were actually concurrent with another
Wall-clock order proves the writes were never concurrent with one another
Some writes are inevitably lost, because each client works from stale data

questions.explanation: The arrows show which operation knew about or depended on which earlier one. Because another operation is always going on concurrently, neither client is ever fully up to date with the server, but each write supersedes exactly the versions its client had read, so old versions do get overwritten eventually and no writes are lost. The server keeps concurrent branches as siblings rather than discarding them.

questions.question: In a single-replica version-number algorithm for detecting concurrent writes, which rules are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The server maintains a version number for every key, increments it every time that key is written, and stores the new version number along with the value written
When a client reads a key, the server returns all values that have not been overwritten, as well as the latest version number. A client must read a key before writing

When a client writes a key it must include the version number from the prior read, and it must merge together all values that it received in the prior read (the response from a write request can be like a read, returning all current values, which allows chaining several writes)
On receiving a write, the server discards every earlier version of that key and retains only the newest value it has so far seen

questions.explanation: The server keeps a version number per key, incremented on every write and stored with the value. A read returns every value not yet overwritten plus the latest version number, and a client must read before writing. A write carries the version number from the prior read and the merge of all values that read returned. The server then overwrites all values with that version number or below, since they have been merged into the new value, but must keep any values with a higher version number, because those are concurrent with the incoming write; discarding everything but the newest value would destroy those siblings. The server decides concurrency from version numbers alone, without interpreting the value, and a write with no version number is concurrent with all others, so it overwrites nothing.

optionExplanations.a: A per-key increasing version records the causal generation of each accepted value and gives later writes metadata with which to supersede earlier versions.
optionExplanations.b: Returning every non-overwritten sibling lets the client observe concurrent branches, while requiring a prior read gives its next write a causal version context.
optionExplanations.c: The client merges the siblings it observed and echoes their version context, allowing the server to replace exactly those ancestors without erasing unseen concurrent branches.
optionExplanations.d: Keeping only the numerically newest value would discard concurrent siblings; the server may remove versions at or below the supplied context but must retain unrelated newer branches.

questions.question: A shopping cart has two concurrent sibling values, [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] and [eggs, milk, ham]. What does a union merge produce?

options.text: [milk, flour, eggs, bacon, ham], with each item appearing once
[eggs, milk, ham], because that sibling has the higher version
Seven items, because milk and eggs appear in both siblings
[milk, eggs], the items that are common to both siblings

questions.explanation: Riak calls concurrent values siblings, and the client must merge them. For a cart that only grows, a reasonable approach is to take the union without duplicates. Milk and eggs appear in both siblings even though each was written once, so they must not be duplicated. Picking one sibling by version or timestamp, as last write wins does, would lose items, and intersection would drop items added on only one side.

questions.question: When shopping-cart siblings are merged by taking their union, what goes wrong if users can also remove items, and what is the fix called?

options.text: Removed items reappear; deletions must leave a marker called a tombstone
Added items disappear; each sibling must carry a version vector
Updated items duplicate; the merge must use last write wins
Concurrently added items duplicate; the merge must deduplicate them

questions.explanation: If an item was removed in only one sibling, the union still contains it from the other sibling, so the removed item reappears. To prevent this, the item cannot simply be deleted; the system leaves a deletion marker with a version number, called a tombstone, so the merge knows the item was removed. Because such merging is error-prone, Riak offers CRDT datatypes that merge siblings automatically, including deletions.

questions.question: In leaderless replication, why is a single version number per key insufficient when several replicas accept writes, and what replaces it?

options.text: Concurrent replicas need a counter each per key, forming a version vector
It is sufficient; version vectors are merely a performance optimization
Wall-clock timestamps replace it, because all replicas share one clock
A single global counter shared by every replica in the cluster replaces it

questions.explanation: With several replicas accepting writes concurrently, one counter per key cannot capture which writes each replica has seen. Instead each replica keeps a version number per key, increments its own when processing a write, and tracks the numbers it has seen from other replicas. This collection is a version vector, and it tells a replica which values to overwrite and which to keep as siblings. Clocks are not shared, and a global counter would need coordination.

questions.question: Which version-vector variant does Riak 2.0 use, and what does Riak call the encoded version vector it sends to clients?

options.text: The dotted version vector; Riak calls the encoded string the causal context
The vector clock; Riak calls the encoded string a digest
The Lamport timestamp; Riak calls the encoded string a hint
The hybrid logical clock; Riak calls the encoded string a tombstone

questions.explanation: Riak 2.0 uses the dotted version vector, a variant of version vectors. As with single-replica version numbers, the version vector is sent to clients on reads and must be sent back on writes; Riak encodes it as a string called the causal context. Carrying it lets the database distinguish overwrites from concurrent writes.

questions.question: In leaderless replication, what cross-replica operation do version vectors make safe, and what caveat remains?

options.text: Read from one replica and write to another, while still merging siblings
They make it safe to write to any replica with no siblings ever created
They make reads strongly consistent, with no caveat
They eliminate the need for application-level merging

questions.explanation: The receiving replica can tell which versions the client observed and which writes are concurrent, so switching replicas does not silently overwrite unseen data. Safety does not eliminate application-level merging.

questions.question: How do the terms version vector and vector clock relate?

options.text: Often conflated but subtly different; version vectors suit comparing replicas
They are identical terms for exactly the same data structure
Vector clocks, not version vectors, are the right structure for comparing replicas
They are unrelated: a vector clock is a physical clock-synchronization protocol

questions.explanation: The names are often conflated, but version vectors track a version per replica for a data item, while vector clocks are the broader causal-ordering concept. For Dynamo-style conflict detection, 'version vector' is more precise.

questions.question: Which purposes can replication serve? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: High availability — keeping the system running when machines or a datacenter fail
Disconnected operation — allowing work to continue through a network interruption
Lower geographic latency and greater read scalability by serving users and read traffic from replicas
Guaranteed preservation of every acknowledged write even when replication is asynchronous

questions.explanation: Replication supports availability, offline work, geographic latency reduction, and read scalability. Asynchronous followers cannot guarantee that every acknowledged write survives leader loss, but they can absorb read traffic when the application tolerates or controls staleness.

optionExplanations.a: Copies on other machines or sites allow service to continue when one replica or datacenter becomes unavailable, subject to the replication and failover design.
optionExplanations.b: Multi-leader or device-local replicas can accept work during disconnection and exchange changes later, enabling offline or partition-tolerant operation.
optionExplanations.c: Nearby replicas shorten read paths and multiple replicas share read traffic, providing both geographic latency reduction and read-throughput scaling.
optionExplanations.d: With asynchronous propagation, the leader may acknowledge before any follower has the write, so leader loss can still erase recently acknowledged data.
